General rule: which court is territorially competent by default (the defendant's domicile), and what applies when the defendant has no known domicile (last known domicile) or has elected a domicile.
Several defendants: may the plaintiff choose the court of any one of their domiciles?
Real property claims (ownership, possession, real rights, partition of real property, leases of buildings): is the court where the property lies exclusively competent?
Mixed claims (personal and real): court where the property lies.
Torts: is the court where the harmful act occurred competent (offence, quasi-offence, damage caused by the administration), alongside or instead of the defendant's domicile?
Contracts for supplies, works and technical or industrial services: court where the contract was concluded or performed, even if a party does not reside there.
Commercial matters (other than bankruptcy and judicial settlement): court where the promise was made or the goods delivered, or where payment must be made.
Bankruptcy, judicial settlement and disputes between partners: court where the proceedings were opened or where the company has its registered office.
Succession and estate partition: court of the deceased's last domicile.
Divorce, return to the marital home: court of the marital home.
Custody, visitation: court of the custodian's residence.
Maintenance (nafaqa): court of the domicile of the maintenance creditor.
Dowry and household goods disputes, marriage authorisation, kafala, guardianship, absence and disappearance: which court by place (CPCA family chapter).

Labour disputes: court where the employment contract was concluded or performed, or the defendant's domicile; exception: court of the plaintiff's (worker's) residence when the contract ended or was suspended by a work accident or occupational illness.
Social-security disputes: which court by place (special law, from memory: the insured's domicile?).
Medical services: court where the care was given.
Postal items and declared-value consignments: court of the sender's or addressee's domicile.
Insurance claims: court of the insured's domicile or where the insured event occurred (from memory, check).
Urgent matters (référé): court of the place of the incident or where the measure is to be carried out.
Execution difficulties and attachment: court of the place of execution.
Disputes involving public bodies before the ordinary courts (e.g. public vehicles): court of the place of the damage.
Defendant residing abroad: may an Algerian or foreign defendant be sued before Algerian courts for obligations contracted in Algeria or abroad; which court by place then (plaintiff's domicile?).
Clauses conferring jurisdiction on a court not otherwise competent: void and deemed unwritten, except between merchants (and in writing?).
Voluntary appearance: may the parties agree to appear before a judge not territorially competent, by signed declaration?
Is territorial jurisdiction a rule of public order? General rule: no; the plea of territorial incompetence must be raised before any defence on the merits or plea of inadmissibility.

Are the 'exclusive' special rules (real property, family, labour, etc.) of public order, so that the judge raises them of his own motion and a clause cannot derogate from them? Check the texts; likely interpretive.
Material incompetence (by subject) is of public order and raised by the judge of his own motion: distinguish it from territorial incompetence.
What the judge does when he declares himself territorially incompetent: does he name the competent court; is the case referred or must the plaintiff refile?
Effect of filing before a territorially incompetent court on the limitation period (interruption even before an incompetent court, Civil Code).
Specialised commercial courts (2022 reform): their territorial reach is set by regulation; this belongs to the ordinary-court-exits module.

Administrative courts: territorial jurisdiction follows the general rule with special cases (taxes, public works, public contracts, staff disputes, damage by public works); belongs to the ordinary-court-exits module but the boundary must be named.
Court sections (civil, real property, family, social, commercial, maritime, urgent) are a question of organisation, not of territory: belongs to the court-sections module.
Counter-claims and related claims: may they be brought before the court seised of the main claim?
Guarantee claims (appel en garantie): court seised of the original claim.
The petition must name the court; an error of territorial court leads to a judgment of incompetence (not inadmissibility).
Leases of dwellings and professional premises: real-property court where the premises lie; commercial leases: check whether the commercial rule or the real-property rule applies.
Amendments to remember: CPCA (Law 08-09 of 25 February 2008) amended by Law 22-13 of 12 July 2022 (specialised commercial courts, administrative appeal courts).
